title: Health, Safety and Security at the Workplace
unit_name: Part B · Healthy, Safe and Secure Working Environment
short: Hazards, occupational health, electrical and fire safety, security of data.
lede: Unit 4 is definition-plus-example. Hazards and electrical safety are the core.
lens: **10 marks with the rest of Unit 4.** Hazard types + two precautions each.
Data security is part of this unit in the current curriculum — passwords, backups, authorised access.
concepts: **1. Hazard** = anything that can cause harm. **Risk** = chance that the harm will occur.
**2. Types of hazard:** physical (cables, noise, fire), electrical, chemical (cleaner fumes), biological, ergonomic (bad chair), psychosocial (stress, bullying).
**3. Occupational health:** physical and mental wellbeing at work. Fatigue, eye strain and RSI are IT-lab issues.
**4. Electrical safety:** no overloaded sockets, no frayed wires, dry hands, don’t open the SMPS, use earthed plugs, UPS/surge protector.
**5. Fire:** know exits, don’t block them, switch off power, use the **correct extinguisher** (CO2 / dry powder on electrical — not water).
**6. Security:** lock the lab, visitor register, don’t share passwords, lock the screen, authorised software only, backup.
**7. Policy / responsibility:** follow school/lab rules, report hazards, use equipment as trained. Employers provide a safe workplace; employees cooperate.
tricks: - Water on an electrical fire is the classic **wrong** answer.
- Hazard vs accident: hazard is the **potential**; accident is the **event**.
mistakes: - Writing “be careful” with no concrete precaution.
- Mixing this unit with the old “Web Applications and Security” syllabus.

qa.q: Differentiate a hazard and an accident with an IT-lab example.
qa.a: A **hazard** is a potential source of harm (a loose cable across the aisle). An **accident** is the event (a student trips and the monitor falls).

qa.q: List four electrical safety rules for a computer lab.
qa.a: Dry hands; earthed plugs; no overloaded boards; don’t open the power supply; report frayed wires; use a surge protector.

qa.q: What is a hazard? Give two examples from a computer laboratory.
qa.a: A hazard is anything in the workplace that can cause injury or ill health. In a computer laboratory the hazards include a trailing cable that can trip someone, a socket or adapter that is overloaded and can start a fire, a wet floor, and a chair with a broken back that can cause a fall.

qa.q: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk? Give one IT-lab example of each.
a: A hazard is anything that can cause harm — for example, a trailing cable across the lab floor.
Risk is the chance that the harm actually happens — for example, the high risk that someone hurrying between PCs trips over that cable.
Safety work removes hazards first, then reduces the remaining risk with guards, rules and training.

qa.q: A student pours water on a sparking socket. Two mistakes and the correct actions.
qa.a: Water on electrical fire; staying next to a live spark. Instead: don’t touch, switch off mains if safe, alert staff, use CO2/powder extinguisher, evacuate.

qa.q: A student answers “Be careful with electricity” to the question “State three electrical safety precautions in a computer lab”. Why will this score no marks? Give three concrete precautions.
a: The answer is vague. A precaution must name a **specific action** that prevents harm.
Precaution 1: never touch plugs or switches with wet hands, and keep liquids away from the computers.
Precaution 2: report damaged cables and loose sockets at once, and do not overload a socket with many plugs.
(Another: switch off and unplug the equipment before cleaning or repairing it.)

qa.q: List four fire safety rules for a workplace.
a: Keep every fire exit and aisle clear of boxes, cables and furniture, and make sure the exit signs are lit.
Check that fire extinguishers are in place, visible and within their expiry date, and know which type to use for an electrical fire.
Switch off and unplug equipment at the end of the day, and never overload a socket with adapters.
If a fire starts, raise the alarm, cut off the power if it is safe to do so, leave by the marked route without using the lift, and go to the assembly point.

qa.q: List four data-security measures for a school computer lab and explain the purpose of each.
a: Unique passwords per user — so every action can be traced to its author.
Authorised access only — outsiders cannot reach student records or exam files.
Regular backups — a failed disk or ransomware cannot destroy the only copy of practical files.
Locked server and storeroom — physical theft of drives is blocked at the door.

qa.q: Explain four types of workplace hazard with one IT-lab example each.
qa.a: Physical — trailing cables; electrical — open socket; ergonomic — low screen causing neck pain; psychosocial — long hours without a break. Control each: cable covers, close sockets, raise the monitor, timetable breaks.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Lab PCs face a window, chairs don’t adjust, passwords are on sticky notes.

(a) Name three hazard/security issues.
(b) One control for each.
(c) Who should you report this to?
a: (a) Glare (ergonomic), poor posture, password leak (security).
(b) Blinds/position screens, adjustable chairs, unique passwords stored in a password manager / teacher vault — never sticky notes.
(c) Lab teacher / system admin / safety in-charge.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In a computer lab, two exits are blocked by boxes, the fire extinguisher is past its expiry date and a printer cable lies across the walkway.

(a) Identify the three hazards.
(b) Name the type of risk each creates.
(c) State one corrective action for each.
a: (a) The blocked exits, the expired extinguisher and the loose cable.
(b) Blocked exits risk people being trapped in an emergency; the expired extinguisher risks a small fire spreading; the cable risks a fall (a tripping hazard).
(c) Clear the exits and keep them free; replace or recharge the extinguisher; tape the cable down or reroute it along the wall.

qa.q: Name four types of fire extinguisher and say which one should be used on an electrical fire in a computer lab. State the PASS steps for using an extinguisher.
a: Types: water, foam, dry powder and carbon dioxide (CO₂).
Water and foam must **not** be used on an electrical fire, because they conduct electricity and can cause a shock or damage the equipment.
For computers, a **CO₂** extinguisher is best because it leaves no residue; dry powder also works but can harm the electronics.
PASS: **P**ull the pin; **A**im the nozzle at the base of the fire; **S**queeze the handle; **S**weep from side to side.
Also switch off the mains supply if it is safe, and raise the alarm.

mcq.q: A trailing cable is mainly a: (a) 7 C (b) physical hazard (c) query (d) style
mcq.a: **(b) physical hazard.**

mcq.q: On an electrical fire you should not use: (a) CO2 (b) dry powder (c) water (d) the alarm
mcq.a: **(c) water.**

mcq.q: RSI in a data-entry job is mostly: (a) a green job (b) an ergonomic/occupational health issue (c) a primary key (d) mail merge
A sticky note under the keyboard with the password is a failure of: (a) ToC (b) data security (c) Goal Seek (d) grouping
mcq.a: **(b) data security.**

mcq.q: For an electrical fire in a computer lab, the most suitable extinguisher is: (a) water (b) carbon dioxide (CO₂) (c) foam (d) a bucket of sand and water
mcq.a: **(b) carbon dioxide (CO₂).** CO₂ does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue on the equipment.

mcq.q: On seeing a damaged electrical cable in the lab, the first thing to do is to: (a) touch it to check whether it is live (b) wrap it with a wet cloth (c) keep away, switch off the supply if safe, and report it (d) ignore it until the next practical
mcq.a: **(c) keep away, switch off the supply if safe, and report it.** A damaged cable can give a shock or start a fire, so the supply should be cut off and the fault reported.

mcq.q: The first thing to do when a fire is discovered is to: (a) raise the alarm and leave by the marked exit  (b) collect your belongings  (c) use the lift  (d) finish the work you are doing
mcq.a: **(a) raise the alarm and leave by the marked exit.** Never use a lift in a fire.

mcq.q: PPE stands for: (a) Personal Protective Equipment  (b) Public Protection Exercise  (c) Power Protection Equipment  (d) Personal Programme Entry
mcq.a: **(a) Personal Protective Equipment.** Gloves, goggles, helmets and safety shoes are examples.

trend: Hazard types, electrical/fire rules, or password/backup security.
onepager: - Hazard = potential; accident = event; risk = chance.
- Types: physical, electrical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychosocial.
- Electrical: dry, earthed, no overload; never water on electrical fire.
- Security: locks, passwords, authorised access, backup.
task: Walk your computer lab and list five hazards with one control each. Include at least one electrical and one ergonomic.
formulas: Hazard = something that can hurt; **Risk** = how likely and how badly
PPE: Personal Protective Equipment — gloves, goggles, masks, ear plugs, safety shoes
Safety sign colours: **red** prohibition/fire, **yellow** warning, **blue** mandatory, **green** emergency
Report every near-miss — a near-miss today is an accident tomorrow
steps: 1. Look around the workplace and **list what could hurt someone** — cables, wet floors, hot surfaces.
2. Judge each hazard: how likely, and how bad. Fix the **high risk** ones first.
3. Remove or guard the hazard, and wear the **PPE** that the task requires.
4. **Report** anything you cannot fix yourself, and write it in the logbook.

title: Workplace Quality and Ergonomics
unit_name: Part B · Healthy, Safe and Secure Working Environment
short: Quality of work, 5S, housekeeping, ergonomic posture and workstation setup.
lede: Sit right, arrange the desk, and 5S the lab. This is the “quality measures” chapter.
lens: **Ergonomics of a computer workstation** is the set diagram/answer.
5S (Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain) appears as a 2-mark list.
concepts: **1. Quality of work** in IT: accurate data, readable documents, meeting time, following the house style, checking before submit.
**2. Housekeeping:** clear aisles, labelled cables, no food, bags not in walkways, shut down PCs.
**3. 5S:** Sort (remove extra), Set in order (a place for everything), Shine (clean), Standardise (same method), Sustain (habit).
**4. Ergonomics** designs work to fit the person. Goal: reduce strain, errors and fatigue.
**5. Workstation:** feet flat, knees ~90°, back supported, screen top at eye level, screen an arm’s length away, elbows ~90°, mouse next to keyboard, wrists straight.
**6. 20-20-20 rule:** every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds — reduces eye strain.
**7. Lighting and noise:** no glare on screen, enough light to read paper, headphones or quiet for data-entry accuracy.
tricks: - Screen **top at eye level**, not looking down at a laptop on the lap.
- 5S order is asked as a list — don’t shuffle Shine and Sort.
mistakes: - Drawing the user hunched over a laptop as “correct posture”.
- Defining quality as “working fast” with no accuracy.

qa.q: What is ergonomics? Give two workstation rules.
qa.a: Designing work to fit the person. Rules: screen at eye level, feet flat, back supported, wrists straight, mouse beside the keyboard.

qa.q: Expand 5S.
qa.a: **5S = Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain.** *Sort* removes what is not needed; *Set in order* gives everything a fixed place; *Shine* means cleaning as you go; *Standardise* writes the method down so anyone can follow it; *Sustain* makes it a daily habit. The first three clean the workplace, the last two keep it clean.

qa.q: What is ergonomics and why does it matter when working at a computer?
qa.a: Ergonomics is the science of designing the workplace to fit the person. At a computer it keeps the body comfortable and prevents backache, neck and shoulder pain, eye strain and repetitive strain injury caused by hours of sitting in a wrong posture with badly placed equipment.

qa.q: What are the four features of quality work in IT? Illustrate with a data-entry task.
a: Accurate — every figure matches the source; for example, marks typed without a single digit error.
Complete — nothing is missing; every student's row is filled.
On time — the file is ready before the deadline, not after.
Checked — a second pass (spell-check, totals re-added) proves the first three.

qa.q: Amit’s laptop is on a high table, he looks up, and his wrists bend on the edge. Two injuries this invites and two fixes.
qa.a: Neck strain and wrist RSI. Fixes: raise the chair or lower the desk, laptop stand + external keyboard, wrist straight, breaks.

qa.q: A student draws a person hunched over a laptop on a low sofa and labels it “correct posture”. Correct this, and give four features of a correct sitting posture at a computer.
a: It is incorrect: a hunched back and a low screen strain the neck, back and wrists.
Feet flat on the floor and the back straight and supported by the chair.
Elbows bent at about 90° with the wrists straight, and the top of the screen at or just below eye level.
The screen about an arm’s length (50–70 cm) away, with short breaks every 20–30 minutes.

qa.q: Describe a correct workstation arrangement and the working habit that prevents strain.
a: Sit back in a chair that supports the lower back, with both feet flat on the floor and knees at about a right angle.
Keep the top of the screen at or just below eye level, about an arm's length away, with the keyboard and mouse close enough to keep the forearms horizontal and the wrists straight.
Place the document you are copying beside the screen rather than flat on the desk, so the neck does not keep turning.
Follow the 20-20-20 habit: every 20 minutes look 20 feet away for 20 seconds, and take a short break and stretch every hour.

qa.q: Explain the 5S method with one computer-lab example for each S.
a: Sort — remove what is not needed: discard dried pens and broken CDs from the lab drawers.
Set in order — give everything a place: label each shelf, cable and software CD.
Shine — clean regularly: wipe keyboards and screens on a fixed weekly roster.
Standardise — make it a rule: the same layout and cleaning checklist in every lab.
Sustain — keep it going: a monthly audit so the lab never slides back.

qa.q: Describe a correct computer workstation and two quality checks before submitting a practical file.
qa.a: Chair and desk so elbows and knees are about 90°, screen arm’s length, top at eye level, no glare. Quality: proof-read, spell-check, file named as asked, print preview, backup copy.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A lab has tangled wires, unmarked CDs, glare, and students skip spell-check.

(a) Map each problem to 5S or ergonomics or quality.
(b) One action each.
(c) Why quality matters in a data-entry job role.
a: (a) Wires/CDs → 5S Set in order; glare → ergonomics; skip spell-check → quality.
(b) Cable ties + labels; blinds or move screens; compulsory preview + peer check.
(c) Wrong data costs money and trust — the job role is Domestic Data Entry Operator.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In a computer lab, cables lie tangled on the floor, unused CDs are piled on the desks and folders have no labels.

(a) Which 5S step removes the unused CDs?
(b) Which step covers labelling the folders and arranging the cables?
(c) Name the remaining steps and say what each means.
a: (a) **Sort**: remove what is not needed.
(b) **Set in order**: a place for everything, with labels, so that things can be found quickly.
(c) **Shine** (clean the area and equipment regularly), **Standardise** (make rules so that the same order is kept) and **Sustain** (make the habit continue).

qa.q: What is housekeeping? Describe five housekeeping rules for a computer lab and explain how they improve safety and quality of work.
a: Housekeeping means keeping the workplace clean, tidy and organised.
Keep floors and walkways clear and store cables neatly, which prevents trips and falls.
Do not eat or drink near the computers, and dust the equipment regularly, which prevents damage and faults.
Label folders, media and equipment and put things back in their place, so that work is found easily and not lost.
Dispose of waste correctly and report faults at once; a clean, orderly lab lets people work accurately and safely.

mcq.q: The first S in 5S is: (a) Shine (b) Sort (c) Sustain (d) Speed
mcq.a: **(b) Sort.**

mcq.q: Screen top should be: (a) at knee level (b) at eye level (c) behind you (d) on the floor
mcq.a: **(b) at eye level.**

mcq.q: 20-20-20 is for: (a) macros (b) eye strain (c) primary keys (d) mail merge
mcq.a: **(b) eye strain.**

mcq.q: Quality in data entry mainly means: (a) speed only (b) accuracy and completeness as well as speed (c) colourful fonts (d) loud music

Ergonomics is the study of: (a) writing computer programs (b) repairing electronic circuits (c) storing data in a database (d) designing workplaces and equipment to suit the user, for comfort, safety and efficiency
mcq.a: **(d) designing workplaces and equipment to suit the user, for comfort, safety and efficiency.** Good ergonomics reduces strain and injury and helps people work better.

mcq.q: For correct posture, the top of the computer screen should be: (a) well above the head (b) on the floor (c) at the level of the keyboard (d) at or slightly below eye level
mcq.a: **(d) at or slightly below eye level.** This lets the user look slightly down without bending the neck.

mcq.q: The 5S workplace method consists of: (a) Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain  (b) Sit, See, Save, Stop, Start  (c) Safety, Speed, Size, Skill, System  (d) Scan, Send, Store, Sell, Sort
mcq.a: **(a) Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain.** It comes from Japanese workplace practice.

mcq.q: Repetitive Strain Injury is caused mainly by: (a) repeating the same small movement for long periods  (b) a single heavy fall  (c) loud noise  (d) cold weather
mcq.a: **(a) repeating the same small movement for long periods.** Typing and mouse work without breaks are common causes.

onepager: - Quality = accurate, complete, on time, checked.
- 5S: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain.
- Ergonomics: 90° elbows/knees, screen eye-level, arm’s length.
task: Photograph or sketch your study desk. Mark three ergonomic faults and the fix for each.
formulas: 5S: **Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain**
Ergonomics = fitting the work to the person, not the person to the work
Screen: arm's length away, top of the screen at or just below eye level
Quality = doing it right the first time; **KAIZEN** = small improvements, every day
steps: 1. **Sort** your desk — keep only what the job needs, remove the rest.
2. **Set in order** — a fixed place for each item, the used-often items closest.
3. Adjust the chair, screen and keyboard so elbows are at **90°** and the screen is at eye level.
4. Every 30 minutes, look 6 metres away for 20 seconds and **stretch** — the 20-20-20 rule.

title: Prevent Accidents and Emergencies
unit_name: Part B · Healthy, Safe and Secure Working Environment
short: Causes of accidents, evacuation, first aid, emergency numbers and incident reporting.
lede: Last chapter of IT 402. Evacuation steps and first aid for cuts, burns and shock.
lens: **Evacuation order** and **first aid don’ts** are the 2–3 markers.
Know: assembly point, don’t use lifts, report incidents even if small.
concepts: **1. Causes of accidents:** unsafe conditions (wet floor, bad wiring) and unsafe acts (running, bypassing rules). Most lab accidents are preventable.
**2. Prevention:** training, PPE where needed, maintenance, 5S, no horseplay, report near-misses.
**3. Emergency types:** fire, electric shock, medical, earthquake, data breach.
**4. Evacuation:** alarm → save work if safe and seconds allow → leave bags → nearest **stairs**, not lift → assembly point → headcount → don’t re-enter.

**5. First aid principles:** protect yourself, call for help, don’t move a seriously injured person, CPR only if trained, cool a burn with water (not ice/toothpaste), for shock switch off power **before** touching.
**6. Electric shock:** switch off mains, use a non-conductor to separate, call help, recovery position if breathing.
**7. Reporting:** date, time, place, names, what happened, injuries, witnesses, action taken. Near-misses count — they prevent the next accident.
**8. Numbers:** school office, local fire, ambulance 112 (India emergency). Keep them posted in the lab.
tricks: - **Power off before touch** is the electric-shock line examiners want.
- Near-miss reporting is a quality/safety behaviour, not “telling on someone”.
mistakes: - Applying toothpaste or ice directly on a burn.
- Using the lift during a fire drill.

qa.q: List four steps of evacuation in the correct order.
qa.a: Hear the alarm → leave via stairs (not lift) → go to the assembly point → answer the headcount and wait for the all-clear.

qa.q: Why report a near-miss?
qa.a: A near-miss shows a hazard that almost caused harm. Reporting it lets the school fix the condition before someone is actually injured.

qa.q: What is an emergency, and what should a workplace emergency plan contain?
qa.a: An emergency is an unexpected event that threatens life, health or property, such as a fire, an earthquake, a chemical spill or a sudden illness. A plan should name the escape routes and the assembly point, the person responsible for each task, the emergency telephone numbers, the location of first-aid kits and extinguishers, and how often evacuation drills will be held.

qa.q: What is the difference between an accident and a near-miss? Why must both be reported?
qa.a: An accident is an event that causes harm — for example, a shock from a damaged cable. A near-miss is an event that could have caused harm but did not — for example, spotting the same damaged cable before anyone touched it. Both must be reported because the near-miss reveals the hazard while there is still time to fix it.

qa.q: The fire alarm rings. A student runs back for a USB and takes the lift. Two wrong actions and the correct ones.
qa.a: Going back for belongings and using the lift. Correct: leave immediately by stairs, USB can be replaced, assemble for headcount.

qa.q: A student says that toothpaste or ice should be put on a minor burn. Correct this and give the right first aid.
a: Toothpaste, butter and ice must **not** be put on a burn; they can damage the skin or cause infection.
Hold the burn under cool running water for about 10–20 minutes.
Then cover it loosely with a clean, non-sticky dressing, do not burst any blisters, and get medical help if the burn is large or deep.

qa.q: Describe the first aid for a minor burn and for a person who has fainted.
a: For a minor burn: hold the area under cool running water for about ten minutes, remove rings or tight clothing near it, cover it with a clean, non-sticky cloth, and do not apply ice, oil or ointment and do not break blisters.
For fainting: lay the person flat on their back, raise the legs above the level of the heart, loosen tight clothing and keep the airway clear.
Do not crowd around, do not throw water on the face and do not give anything to drink until the person is fully conscious.
Call for medical help if the person does not recover within a minute or if breathing is not normal.

qa.q: What should a workplace emergency plan contain? List its essential parts with one line on each.
a: Alarm and exits — how the alarm sounds and which stairs and exits to use (never the lift).
Assembly and headcount — where to gather outside and who checks that everyone is out.
First aid and numbers — where the kit is and the emergency number 112 for fire, police and ambulance.
Roles and reporting — who leads the evacuation and how every incident and near-miss is written up afterwards.

qa.q: Explain first aid for (i) a small cut (ii) a minor burn (iii) suspected electric shock.
qa.a: Cut: wash, pressure, clean dressing. Burn: cool with running water 10 minutes, loose sterile cover, no toothpaste/ice. Shock: do not touch until power is off; then separate with a dry non-conductor, call help, monitor breathing.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

During a practical a student gets a shock from a damaged mouse cable, laughs it off, and no one writes it down.

(a) Immediate first actions.
(b) Why a report still matters.
(c) Two prevention steps so it does not recur.
a: (a) Switch off power, check breathing, first aid, inform the teacher.
(b) Near-miss/incident record → cable replaced, others warned, pattern spotted.
(c) Inspect peripherals, remove damaged devices, remind: report all shocks.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

During a practical, smoke rises from a UPS in the lab.

(a) What should the teacher and students do first?
(b) Which emergency numbers can be called?
(c) How should the room be left?
a: (a) Raise the alarm and, if it is safe, switch off the main power supply; do not use water on electrical equipment.
(b) 101 for the fire service, or 112, the national emergency number (100 for police and 102 for an ambulance).
(c) Everyone leaves calmly by the stairs, not the lift, and gathers at the assembly point, where the teacher takes a head count.

qa.q: List five items of a first-aid box and five rules that a first-aider should follow.
a: Items: sterile gauze and bandages, adhesive plasters, antiseptic solution, scissors, and disposable gloves (also cotton wool and a burn dressing).
Rule 1: first make sure the area is safe, for example switch off the power in case of electric shock.
Rule 2: call for help and the emergency number quickly.
Rule 3: do not move a seriously injured person unless there is danger, and reassure them.
Rule 4: wear gloves and wash hands; do not give food or drink to an unconscious person.

mcq.q: During a fire, do not: (a) use stairs (b) go to the assembly point (c) use the lift (d) follow the teacher
mcq.a: **(c) use the lift.**

mcq.q: For electric shock, first: (a) grab the person (b) switch off power (c) pour water (d) apply toothpaste
mcq.a: **(b) switch off power.**

mcq.q: A near-miss should be: (a) ignored (b) reported (c) punished always (d) posted on social media
mcq.a: **(b) reported.**

mcq.q: A minor burn is cooled with: (a) ice cubes rubbed hard (b) running water (c) toothpaste (d) cotton oil
mcq.a: **(b) running water.**

mcq.q: In India, the single national emergency number is: (a) 108 only (b) 112 (c) 1800 (d) 911
mcq.a: **(b) 112.** 112 is the all-in-one emergency number; 101 is for fire, 100 for police and 102 for ambulance.

mcq.q: During a fire drill, people should leave the building using the: (a) lift (b) windows (c) back of the lab (d) stairs
mcq.a: **(d) stairs.** Lifts may stop working or trap people in a fire, so the stairs are used.

mcq.q: The single all-India emergency number for police, fire and ambulance is: (a) 112  (b) 100  (c) 101  (d) 108
mcq.a: **(a) 112.** 100 is police, 101 is fire and 108 is the ambulance service in most states.

mcq.q: During an evacuation you should: (a) walk quickly to the assembly point without using the lift  (b) run and push past others  (c) use the lift to leave faster  (d) go back for your bag
mcq.a: **(a) walk quickly to the assembly point without using the lift.** Report to the assembly point so that everyone can be counted.

trend: Evacuation steps or electric-shock first aid; near-miss as a value item.
onepager: - Accidents = unsafe act + unsafe condition; prevent both.
- Shock: power off, then help. Burns: water, not toothpaste.
task: Write a half-page incident report for a fictional wet-floor slip in the lab: who, when, where, injury, action, prevention.
formulas: Emergency numbers in India: **112** (all-in-one), 101 fire, 102 ambulance, 100 police
First aid for burns: cool running water for 10 minutes — no ice, no ointment, no cotton
Never use water on an **electrical** fire — cut the supply and use a CO₂ or dry-powder extinguisher
steps: 1. Check the scene is **safe for you** before you help anyone — a second casualty helps nobody.
2. Call for help and give the **four facts**: where, what happened, how many hurt, your phone number.
3. Give only the first aid you know: stop bleeding, cool a burn, recover position if unconscious.
4. Stay with the person, keep them calm, and **hand over clearly** when help arrives.
